Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened, Children Present: Being around children
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
The crisis began on a Tuesday in late November, when Julian’s four-year-old son, Leo, collapsed in the kitchen with sudden respiratory distress. For six hours, Julian watched plastic tubes breach his son’s airway while a regional blizzard howled against the hospital’s north-facing windows. News helicopters circled downtown, broadcasting emergency alerts that flooded their phones with updates on overwhelmed wards. That night, Julian believed he had failed to shield Leo from the rapid decline of his breathing. He replayed the exact sequence in his mind—the way the oxygen saturation numbers had dropped, the sound of the ventilator’s initial alarm—but whenever his thoughts pushed toward the moment the doctors finally stabilized him, he forced himself to look away, stopping the recall before it could settle. The images of Leo’s translucent skin and the stark overhead lights remained sharp, etched into his vision whenever he closed his eyes. Over the following months, Julian’s world narrowed. He began scanning every room before he felt safe, counting doors and fire exits until he could finally sit. At work as a financial analyst, he requested a desk near the stairwell, far from the lobby where corporate newsletters sometimes highlighted pediatric health initiatives. When a colleague’s toddler wandered into the open-plan office during a family day, Julian found himself backing into the copy room, his pulse hammering as if the child’s laughter signaled an emergency. He never finished explaining his reaction to Clara. He had come to believe that his own hypervigilance was the only thing standing between Leo and another crisis, a certainty that kept him awake long after she fell asleep. He listened to the house settling, to the distant hum of traffic, waiting for any sound that might indicate danger. What frightened Julian most was how his own body had turned against him. A dropped coffee mug in the breakroom sent him lurching upright, heart racing as though alarms were already blaring. He stopped attending client dinners because he could never be sure of a quick exit, and he began leaving family gatherings early. Clara felt the distance solidify; when he caught his reflection in the office kitchen, he barely recognized the man staring back. The husband who once made spontaneous plans now calculated sightlines and monitored weather apps with quiet desperation. When the wind matched the velocity of that hospital night, his chest tightened and his hands trembled until he could check the news and confirm no regional emergencies were unfolding. By the time Julian sat in the therapist’s office, he had exhausted himself tracking every new safety ritual. He finally agreed to seek help after Clara quietly suggested counseling, her voice steady but frayed at the edges, and after he realized he could no longer pretend his reactions were simply stress. He wanted to understand why he felt like a stranger to himself, why his mind kept returning to the ICU monitors, and whether he could ever sit in a park with Leo without bracing for impact. He was hoping, more than anything, to find a way to trust that the danger had passed, even when his body insisted it was still there.
